evidence_1.statement: Higher SNAP household concentration indicates greater community-level economic vulnerability.
evidence_1.relevance: Economic instability can create barriers to maintaining healthcare access and meeting basic needs.

evidence_2.statement: A higher proportion of households receiving public assistance indicates greater economic vulnerability.
evidence_2.relevance: Economic vulnerability may affect the ability to meet basic needs and maintain consistent healthcare access.

evidence_3.statement: Higher poverty prevalence indicates greater community-level economic vulnerability.
evidence_3.relevance: Poverty can create financial barriers to healthcare, transportation, housing, nutrition, and other basic needs.

evidence_4.statement: A higher proportion of adults with less than a ninth-grade education indicates lower educational attainment.
evidence_4.relevance: Lower educational attainment may create barriers to health literacy, healthcare navigation, and understanding health information.

evidence_5.statement: A higher proportion of adults completing ninth through twelfth grade without a diploma indicates lower educational attainment.
evidence_5.relevance: Lower educational attainment can affect health literacy and ability to navigate healthcare resources.

evidence_6.statement: High-school educational attainment provides an indicator of community educational resources and attainment.
evidence_6.relevance: Educational attainment is associated with the ability to understand and navigate health information.

evidence_7.statement: College educational attainment provides a community-level indicator of educational opportunity.
evidence_7.relevance: Educational opportunity can influence health literacy, employment opportunities, and healthcare navigation.

evidence_8.statement: A higher proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher indicates greater educational attainment.
evidence_8.relevance: Educational attainment provides contextual information about community-level health literacy and socioeconomic opportunity.

evidence_9.statement: A higher uninsured population indicates reduced access to healthcare coverage.
evidence_9.relevance: Lack of insurance can create financial barriers to preventive care, treatment, and continuity of care.

evidence_10.statement: Higher uninsured prevalence within the community indicates greater potential healthcare access vulnerability.
evidence_10.relevance: Uninsured populations may experience greater financial barriers to healthcare services.

evidence_11.statement: Routine checkup prevalence provides an indicator of preventive healthcare utilization.
evidence_11.relevance: Lower preventive-care utilization may indicate barriers to routine healthcare engagement.

evidence_12.statement: Cholesterol screening prevalence provides an indicator of preventive healthcare engagement.
evidence_12.relevance: Lower screening utilization may indicate barriers to preventive healthcare access.

evidence_13.statement: A higher proportion of renter households spending 30 to 34.9 percent of income on rent indicates increased housing cost burden.
evidence_13.relevance: Housing cost burden can reduce resources available for healthcare, transportation, food, and other basic needs.

evidence_14.statement: A higher proportion of renter households spending 35 percent or more of income on rent indicates substantial housing cost burden.
evidence_14.relevance: High housing costs can contribute to financial instability and reduce resources available for healthcare.

evidence_15.statement: A higher proportion of households with moderate overcrowding indicates increased housing pressure.
evidence_15.relevance: Crowded housing conditions can affect health, privacy, stress, and exposure to illness.

evidence_16.statement: A higher proportion of severely overcrowded households indicates significant housing pressure.
evidence_16.relevance: Severe overcrowding may increase health risks and indicate housing instability.

evidence_17.statement: Housing vacancy provides contextual information about the local housing environment.
evidence_17.relevance: Housing market conditions can influence neighborhood stability and access to appropriate housing.

evidence_18.statement: A higher renter population provides contextual information about housing tenure within a community.
evidence_18.relevance: Housing tenure can provide context for housing stability and potential exposure to rental cost pressures.

evidence_19.statement: A higher number of households without a vehicle indicates greater potential transportation vulnerability.
evidence_19.relevance: Limited vehicle access may make it harder to reach healthcare services, employment, food, and community resources.

evidence_20.statement: A higher low-access population indicates greater geographic transportation barriers to essential services.
evidence_20.relevance: Transportation barriers may reduce access to healthcare and other essential community resources.

evidence_21.statement: Households without vehicles located beyond accessible driving distances may face increased transportation barriers.
evidence_21.relevance: Limited transportation options can make healthcare access and appointment attendance more difficult.

evidence_22.statement: SNAP households located in low-access areas may face combined economic and transportation barriers.
evidence_22.relevance: Combined economic and transportation barriers can compound difficulty accessing healthcare and basic resources.

evidence_23.statement: Households without vehicles located beyond accessible straight-line distances may face transportation barriers.
evidence_23.relevance: Transportation limitations may interfere with healthcare access and continuity of care.

evidence_24.statement: SNAP households experiencing geographic access limitations may face combined socioeconomic and transportation barriers.
evidence_24.relevance: Multiple barriers can compound difficulty accessing healthcare and community resources.

evidence_25.statement: A higher number of low-income, low-access census tracts indicates increased geographic transportation vulnerability.
evidence_25.relevance: Low-access areas may experience reduced ability to reach healthcare and essential services.

evidence_26.statement: A higher number of low-vehicle-access tracts indicates greater community transportation vulnerability.
evidence_26.relevance: Low vehicle access can limit healthcare and essential-service access.

evidence_27.statement: Low-income, low-access areas indicate combined socioeconomic and geographic vulnerability.
evidence_27.relevance: Combined socioeconomic and transportation barriers can reduce access to healthcare.

evidence_28.statement: Low vehicle access at the tract level indicates increased transportation vulnerability.
evidence_28.relevance: Limited vehicle access may create barriers to healthcare appointments and essential services.

evidence_29.statement: Computer access provides an indicator of community digital connectivity.
evidence_29.relevance: Limited computer access may reduce the ability to use digital healthcare services and health information.

evidence_30.statement: Broadband access provides an indicator of community digital connectivity.
evidence_30.relevance: Limited broadband access can restrict telehealth and digital healthcare access.

evidence_31.statement: Higher asthma prevalence indicates greater community-level respiratory health burden.
evidence_31.relevance: Elevated respiratory disease burden may indicate increased need for community health resources.

evidence_32.statement: Higher COPD prevalence indicates greater community-level respiratory disease burden.
evidence_32.relevance: Respiratory disease burden may increase the need for chronic disease and community health support.

evidence_33.statement: Higher diabetes prevalence indicates greater community-level chronic disease burden.
evidence_33.relevance: Elevated chronic disease burden may indicate increased need for prevention and community health resources.

evidence_34.statement: Higher heart disease prevalence indicates greater community cardiovascular disease burden.
evidence_34.relevance: Higher cardiovascular disease burden may increase the need for preventive and chronic disease support.

evidence_35.statement: Higher obesity prevalence indicates greater community-level metabolic health burden.
evidence_35.relevance: Elevated obesity prevalence can indicate increased need for community wellness and prevention resources.

evidence_36.statement: Higher physical inactivity prevalence indicates greater community-level inactivity burden.
evidence_36.relevance: Physical inactivity may contribute to chronic disease risk and indicates potential need for wellness resources.

evidence_37.statement: Higher prevalence of poor mental health indicates greater community-level mental health burden.
evidence_37.relevance: Community mental health burden may indicate increased need for behavioral-health and community-support resources.

evidence_38.statement: Higher prevalence of poor physical health indicates greater community-level physical health burden.
evidence_38.relevance: Poor physical health burden may indicate increased need for healthcare navigation and community support.

evidence_39.statement: Higher smoking prevalence indicates greater community-level tobacco-use burden.
evidence_39.relevance: Smoking burden may indicate increased need for prevention and health-behavior support.

evidence_40.statement: Higher stroke prevalence indicates greater community-level cardiovascular health burden.
evidence_40.relevance: Higher stroke burden may indicate increased need for preventive and chronic-care resources.
